Q104173756.summary: Under a row of gabled and arched canopies carried on twisted columns, seven bearded and robed figures stand in niches. In the central niche Christ raises his right hand as he teaches, a box of scrolls (scrinium) at his feet, while the apostles around him hold scrolls and books or turn toward one another. The scrolls, borrowed from Roman imagery, signified knowledge of the true faith received from Christ the teacher.
facts: The chest was reused in the Middle Ages as a lintel over the door of the church of Saint-Michel-du-Touch, north of Toulouse; only the front and the beginnings of the short sides survive.
In 1777 local antiquaries took its figures for the decurions who formed the senate of Roman Toulouse.
The museum displays it with the 'Queen Pédauque' lid, which very probably belongs to it but was itself reused as a lintel at the church of La Daurade.
Q104173756.notes: The museum mentions a scrinium at Christ's feet and at those of the apostle in the last arcade on the left; the thumbnail shows boxes in the first and fourth niches. Christ is identified by position and gesture per the museum's description; he is not haloed.

cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-thyatir.summary: Christ, haloed and holding a cross-staff, looks out from a band of blue sky at the top left; below, John sits writing on a long scroll while an angel stands before a temple-like church, and armed men with spears gather on either side.
facts: The Trier Apocalypse contains 74 full-page drawings illustrating about 150 episodes of the Book of Revelation; it is one of the earliest illustrated Apocalypse manuscripts to survive.
Its pictures are thought to copy a late antique model of the 4th–6th century, which explains features such as books shown as scrolls and Christ as the beardless Logos.
cur:manuscripts-trier-apocalypse-thyatir.notes: The Commons description assigns this page to the letter to Thyatira; because the early pictures of this manuscript sit on the verso after the text they illustrate and often combine episodes, the exact letter is not certain.

cur:objects-genoels-elderen-diptych-chri.summary: A tall, frontal Christ, flanked by two angels, carries a cross over his shoulder and a book, and stands upon a lion and a serpent-like dragon. A Latin inscription runs across the top of the frame, and the surrounding border is filled with interlace and inlaid blue glass. The plaque illustrates Psalm 91, read as a prophecy of Christ trampling the powers of evil; its companion leaf shows the Annunciation and the Visitation.
facts: Wikipedia's article on the theme lists it among the few works showing Christ treading on the beasts, describing it as 'either a much more provincial version of Carolingian style, or Northumbrian', with four beasts.
The museum label attributes the two plaques, found at Genoels-Elderen in Belgium, perhaps to the Rhine–Meuse region in the late 8th century.

cur:objects-genoels-elderen-diptych-chri.notes: Wikipedia speaks of four beasts; in the photograph a lion and a dragon/serpent are clearly visible beneath Christ's feet.
